pronunciation.body:

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**hebe** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Hebe.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Hebe" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Hebe" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"hebe" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Hebe ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Hebe ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌Hebe ‌place ​youth, cupbearer ​at ​the ​center of ​a ‌living ​mythological world.

### ​Origins ‌(Myth)

​Hebe appears ‌in ​greek ‌tradition as ​youth, ​cupbearer. The ​name's ​meaning, ​"Youth (from ‌ἥβη)", ​shapes ‌the narratives ​told ‌about ​this figure.

### ‌Worship ​and ‌Memory (Cult)

​Devotees ​and ‌later tradition-keepers ‌preserved ‌Hebe in ​ritual, ​text, ‌and iconography, ​ensuring ​the ‌name survived ​into ​the ‌modern scholarly ​record.

‌The ​myths of ​Hebe ​survive ​in fragments, ‌summaries, ‌and ​later retellings. ‌Each ​version reflects ​the ‌interests ‌of its ‌tellers ‌— ​poets, priests, ‌philosophers, ​and ​scholars. The ​PuniCodex ‌entry ​does not ​privilege ​a ‌single version; ​it ​gathers the ​attestations ‌so ​that readers ‌can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌Hebe ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Ἥβη, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​youth ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

overview.body:
**Hebe** ​(*hebe*) — ‌Youth, Cupbearer ‌· ​Youth (from ​ἥβη) — ​belongs ​to the ​Greek tradition, ‌where ​it is ​catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Youth, ‌Cupbearer". ​The name ‌means "Youth ​(from ​ἥβη)"[^1].

**Hebe** ​is youth ​in ​its most ‌literal Greek ​sense ‌— ἥβη, ​the bloom ‌of ​early strength ‌— ​made goddess: ‌cupbearer of ​Olympus, ​wife of ‌the deified ‌Herakles, ‌and the ​only figure ​in ‌the pantheon ​whose name ​**is** ‌her domain. ​Hers is ​a ‌small mythology ​with ‌a large ​office: keeping ​the ​immortals fed, ​and keeping ‌the ‌idea of ​youth itself ‌enthroned.[^2]

​PuniCodex records ​the canonical ‌scholarly ‌spelling **Hebe** ‌and serves ‌its ​temple at ‌[its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/hebe/). The ​displayed form ​is ‌ASCII-equivalent — ​a description ​computed ​from the ‌displayed form ​itself. ​The plain ​ASCII form ‌*hebe* ​contains the ‌same letters: ​no ‌recovered diacritics ​or ‌special encoding ‌is claimed. ​The ​work here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Greek ​as ​**Ἥβη**. Etymologically ​it ​means ​"Youth (from ‌ἥβη)"[^1].

​The canonical ​spelling ‌**Hebe** matches ​the ‌conventional scholarly ​romanization. ‌The plain ​ASCII ​form *hebe* ​contains ​the same ​letters, ‌so ​no lost ‌diacritics ​or encoding ‌transition ​is claimed. ‌The ​editorial work ‌is ​to fix ​one ‌reviewed reference ‌spelling, ‌preserve capitalization ​and ​provenance, ‌and keep ​the ​original evidence ‌visible. ​The displayed ​form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a description ​computed ​from the ​displayed ​form itself.

‌The ‌letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

- ‌**h** ​→ **H** ​— ‌Rough breathing
- ‌**e** ‌→ **e** ‌— ​Short epsilon
- ‌**b** ​→ **b** ​— ​Beta
- **e** ‌→ ​**e** ​— Short ​epsilon

‌Attested and ​derived ​spellings of ​the ‌name:

- **Hḗbe** ​— ‌ideal form: ​Stacked ‌macron+acute on ​the ‌stressed long ‌vowel, ​matching ​Greek Ἥβη; ​philologically ​ideal but ‌often ‌untypeable on ​phones.

meditation.body: Hebe ​is the ‌goddess of ‌what ​no one ​keeps. Youth, ​in the ​Greek ​imagination, is ‌not a ​stage ​you remember; ‌it is ​a ‌substance the ​gods drink. ‌That ​is why ​the mythology ​gives the ​youngest ​goddess the ‌most repetitive ​job ‌on Olympus ​— pouring, ‌refilling, ​pouring again ‌— and ​why ‌the only ​city that ​built her ‌a ‌temple was ‌a small ​one, ​Phlius (Pausanias ‌2.13.3). Some ​gifts ​are so ‌universal they ​escape ​notice; some ‌are so ​brief they ‌deserve ​a permanent ​address. Her ​marriage ​to Herakles ‌completes the ‌thought. ​The hero ‌who burned ​off ​his mortality ‌did not ‌receive wisdom, ‌or ‌prophecy, or ​wealth — ‌he ​received youth, ​forever, in ​the ‌person of ​its goddess. ​To ​be made ‌a god, ​in this ​telling, ​is precisely ‌to stop ​losing ‌ἥβη. It ​is the ‌Greek ​answer to ‌every human ‌grief: ​not that ​youth returns, ​but that ​somewhere ‌it never ‌left the ​table.[^1]
